paragraphs.heading: Blocking an enzyme
paragraphs.text: Enzymes are proteins that speed up the chemical reactions life depends on, turning starting molecules, called substrates, into products. Each enzyme grabs its substrate at a special spot called the active site, where the hardest step of the reaction is made easier. An enzyme inhibitor is a molecule that latches onto an enzyme and shuts down its activity. It can sit in the active site so the substrate cannot get in, or it can attach somewhere else on the enzyme and still stop the reaction.

paragraphs.heading: Why cells use them
paragraphs.text: Inhibitors matter in every cell, because each one usually targets a single enzyme and keeps its activity in check. In a chain of reactions, an enzyme can be slowed by molecules made further along the chain, so the cell stops making what it no longer needs. This kind of negative feedback helps keep conditions inside the cell steady. Inhibitors also hold back enzymes such as proteases and nucleases, which could harm the cell if they ran unchecked.

paragraphs.heading: Poisons and medicines
paragraphs.text: Many poisons made by plants and animals work by blocking vital enzymes in prey or predators. Many medicines work the same way, aimed at a faulty human enzyme or at an enzyme a virus, bacterium or parasite needs to survive. Methotrexate, used in chemotherapy and for rheumatic arthritis, is one example, and so are the protease inhibitors used against HIV/AIDS. Finding and improving enzyme inhibitors is a busy field in biochemistry and drug research.

paragraphs.heading: Small molecules and proteins
paragraphs.text: Inhibitors come in many chemical forms, from small organic molecules to large proteins. The best-known protein inhibitors are serpins, which animals make to stop enzymes switching on at the wrong time and plants make to fend off being eaten. Some enzymes even carry their own built-in blocker. These precursors, called zymogens, have a piece at one end that plugs the active site, and another enzyme must cut that piece off before the enzyme becomes active.

paragraphs.heading: Where the inhibitor binds
paragraphs.text: Most often an inhibitor binds the same site as the substrate; these are called orthosteric inhibitors. They work simply by competing with the substrate, so the enzyme cannot convert it into product. Allosteric inhibitors bind at a site away from the active site instead. They may change the enzyme's shape so it can no longer hold the substrate, or let the substrate bind but lock the enzyme in a shape that cannot do the reaction.

paragraphs.heading: Reversible or not
paragraphs.text: An irreversible inhibitor forms a chemical bond with the enzyme, and the enzyme stays blocked until that bond breaks. A reversible inhibitor holds on through weaker forces such as hydrogen bonds and ionic bonds, and it can drift off and let the enzyme work again. Many of these weak bonds together make the grip strong and specific. Reversible inhibitors usually do not react with the enzyme while bound, and they can be removed easily by dilution or dialysis.

paragraphs.heading: Winning the competition
paragraphs.text: Reversible inhibitors are sorted by how they change two numbers as the amount of substrate is varied. Vₘₐₓ is the top rate the enzyme can reach, and Kₘ is the substrate concentration that gives half of that top activity. In competitive inhibition, the substrate and the inhibitor cannot both be bound at once, since they compete for the active site. Adding enough substrate can overcome this, so Vₘₐₓ stays the same, but it takes more substrate to reach half that rate, so the apparent Kₘ goes up. Competitive inhibitors often look a lot like the real substrate.
